newsitem.title: USA: Fed looks set to raise interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Fed looks set to raise interest rates.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The Federal Reserve Board looked set to raise interest rates on Tuesday for the first time in more than two years, in a bid to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep the economic expansion on track, analysts said.
With growth strong and jobs plentiful, analysts said the inflation-wary central bank was likely to decide that it had less to lose by raising rates than leaving them unchanged.
"The case for a tightening (of credit) is a pretty good one," said Joel Prakken, chairman of St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers. "The chances of it are pretty high."

Financial markets were primed for a quarter percentage point rate increase by the Fed. After sagging last week in anticipation of tighter credit, the Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares soared 100.46 points on Monday.
Analysts said investors were looking beyond Tuesday's expected rate increase and anticipating a continuation of the economic expansion, which turned six years old this month.

The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee was scheduled to begin its policy-making meeting at 9 a.m. EST (1400 GMT). It was expected to announce its rate decision sometime around 2:15 p.m. (1915 GMT).
A rate increase would be the Fed's first since Feb. 1995 and would mean higher borrowing costs for everyone from consumers using credit cards to companies financing inventory.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan laid the groundwork last week for higher rates by stressing the importance to the economy of keeping inflation down.

"If we allow that to get away, we will at the end of the day find that we have set in motion a set of forces which bring the long, sustainable, stable recovery to an end," the central bank chief told Congress's Joint Economic Committee.
He pointed to the tight labor market in particular as a potential source of concern, voicing worries that it could lead to excessive wage demands and rising inflation.
Many lawmakers, though, seemed unconvinced and questioned why rates should be raised now when inflation is low.
"If the Fed goes ahead and pulls the trigger, you're going to see a real outcry," said Roger Hickey, co-director of the Campaign for America's Future, a liberal think tank in Washington.

He said President Bill Clinton should sprearhead the political protest against any Fed rate increase. "It's better for the next recession to be known as the Greenspan recession than the Clinton one," he said.

For their part, Clinton administration officials do not seem all that concerned about the possibility of a modest rate increase by the independent central bank because they believe the economy is strong enough to withstand it.

After expanding at a brisk 3.9 percent annualized pace in the fourth quarter of last year, the economy looks to have slowed slightly in the first three months of this year to a growth rate closer to 3 percent, analysts said.
With the economy enjoying strong momentum, many analysts believe that the central bank will need to raise rates more than once to keep inflation in check.
"This will not be the last tightening," said James Griffith, senior vice president at Aeltus Invesment Management of Hartford, Connecticut.

He maintained Greenspan has trained his sights on the stock market -- the Fed chief suggested last month that equity prices may be too high -- and said that too argues for further rate increases by the central bank.
Other analysts were not so sure. Prakken said he expects the economy to slow further in the months ahead -- whether or not the central bank raises rates on Tuesday.
The Fed has not changed monetary policy since Jan. 31, 1996, when it cut rates by a quarter percentage point.

Its target for the federal funds rate -- the rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans -- stands at 5.25 percent. Its discount rate -- the rate it charges the banks for money -- is 5.0 percent.
